nameStory: This marine snail gets its charming name from its unique shell shape that looks exactly like a tiny teacup sitting on a saucer. The cone-shaped shell has a flat, plate-like base that spreads out around it, creating the perfect miniature tableware for a fairy tea party. The word 'striatum' in its scientific name refers to the fine ridges or stripes that decorate the shell surface.
description: The cup-and-saucer limpet is a small sea snail that creates one of the ocean's most distinctive shells. Unlike typical spiral snail shells, this creature builds a cone-shaped 'cup' that sits atop a flat, circular 'saucer' base. The entire shell is usually white to pale gray and small enough to fit comfortably on your thumbnail. As a marine gastropod mollusk, it's related to garden snails but has adapted completely to life in saltwater.

idTips.label: Cup-and-saucer shape
idTips.description: The unmistakable shell has a tall, pointed cone sitting in the center of a flat, circular base - exactly like a teacup on a saucer when viewed from the side

idTips.label: Fine ridges
idTips.description: Run your finger gently over the surface to feel the delicate radiating ridges that fan out from the apex like spokes on a wheel

idTips.label: White to gray color
idTips.description: The shell is typically chalky white or pale gray, sometimes with a slightly pearlescent interior that catches the light

idTips.label: Small size
idTips.description: The entire shell structure is quite small, usually fitting easily within the circle made by your thumb and forefinger

idTips.label: Attached to hard surfaces
idTips.description: Found firmly cemented to rocks, shells, or pier pilings - they feel solidly attached and require effort to remove

habitat: Cup-and-saucer limpets attach themselves to hard surfaces in New England's intertidal and shallow subtidal zones. Look for them cemented to rocks, shells, pier pilings, and jetties along the coast from Maine to Connecticut. They prefer areas with good water circulation and are often found in tide pools or just below the low tide line.

seasonality.spring: Shells are most easily spotted during spring low tides when winter storms have cleared away loose debris, making attached specimens more visible on cleaned rock surfaces.
seasonality.summer: Peak observation season as calm waters and frequent low tides provide excellent viewing opportunities. Living specimens may be more active during warmer months.
seasonality.fall: Still readily visible, though increasing storm activity may make tide pool exploration more challenging. Empty shells may wash up on beaches.
seasonality.winter: Harder to observe due to rough seas and limited tide pool access, but specimens remain attached year-round. Beach-combing may reveal empty shells after storms.

funFact: Cup-and-saucer limpets are actually filter feeders that create their own tiny dining room - they pump water through their shell and catch microscopic food particles in a net of mucus, essentially turning their beautiful teacup home into a sophisticated cafeteria!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with regular cone-shaped limpets, but remember the key difference: cup-and-saucer limpets have that distinctive flat 'saucer' base extending beyond the cone, while true limpets are just simple domes. Think 'teacup with saucer' versus 'upside-down bowl' and you'll never mix them up.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'limpets,' these creatures aren't true limpets at all - they're actually slipper snails that have evolved a similar cone-shaped lifestyle. True limpets belong to a completely different family, showing how similar ocean environments can shape unrelated animals to look remarkably alike.
compareHints: As the only cup-and-saucer limpet species commonly found in New England waters, it's most easily compared to its slipper snail relatives like the common slipper shell. Unlike slipper shells which have a flat shelf inside a slipper-shaped shell, cup-and-saucer limpets have that distinctive external 'saucer' base. The overall structure is much more three-dimensional and sculptural than the relatively flat profile of slipper shells.
